lectures.title: Rules of procedure in two minutes
lectures.summary: Roll call, quorum, the speakers list, motions, caucuses and voting: the flow of every committee session.

slides.title: Rules of procedure in two minutes
bullets: The flow of every committee session
What to say, and when
say: Hello, and welcome to DelegateDesk.
I'm Meera, and in the next two minutes we'll walk through the rules of procedure that shape every Model UN committee.
By the end, you'll know exactly what happens, in what order, and what you're allowed to say.

slides.title: Roll call and quorum
bullets: Answer "present" or "present and voting"
Present and voting: you cannot abstain on substance
Quorum: enough members to debate
say: Every session starts with roll call.
When your country is called, you answer present, or present and voting.
Present and voting is a promise: you will vote yes or no on resolutions, and you give up the right to abstain.
The chair then checks quorum, which simply means enough delegations are in the room for debate to begin.

slides.title: The general speakers list
bullets: Raise your placard to be added
Usually 60 to 90 seconds each
Yield: to the chair, to questions, or to another delegate
say: Next, the chair opens the general speakers list.
Raise your placard to be added, and wait for your turn.
Speeches are short, usually sixty to ninety seconds.
If you finish early, you yield your remaining time: to the chair, to questions, or to another delegate.

slides.title: Motions
bullets: Moderated caucus: a topic, a total time, a time per speaker
Unmoderated caucus: leave your seats and negotiate
Most disruptive motions are voted first
say: Most of the real work happens in caucuses, and you get there by raising motions.
A moderated caucus needs a topic, a total time and a speaking time, for example ten minutes at one minute each.
An unmoderated caucus lets everyone leave their seats to negotiate and draft.
When several motions are on the floor, the chair votes on the most disruptive one first.

slides.title: Points and rights
bullets: Point of order: a rule was broken
Point of personal privilege: you can't hear, or you're unwell
Right of reply: your country's honour was insulted
say: You can also raise points.
A point of order means a rule was not followed.
A point of personal privilege is about your comfort: you can't hear the speaker, or the room is too cold.
And a right of reply is granted when a speech insulted your country's honour, not just when you disagree.

slides.title: Voting procedure
bullets: Procedural votes: everyone votes, no abstentions
Substantive votes: yes, no or abstain
Simple majority, unless the rules say two thirds
say: Finally, the committee closes debate and moves into voting.
On procedural matters, every delegation votes, and nobody abstains.
On draft resolutions, you vote yes, no, or abstain, unless you said present and voting.
Most resolutions need a simple majority, though some committees require two thirds, and the Security Council has its own rules, including the veto.

slides.title: You're ready
bullets: Roll call → speakers list → motions → voting
Practise in a live session on DelegateDesk
Next: writing your position paper
say: So that's the flow: roll call, the speakers list, motions and caucuses, then voting.
The best way to learn it is to practise, so open a live session on DelegateDesk with a few friends and try chairing.
See you in the next lecture.

lectures.title: Writing a position paper chairs remember
lectures.summary: A four-part structure, the research that matters, and the mistakes that cost marks.

slides.title: Writing a position paper chairs remember
bullets: A structure that works for any committee
Research that actually matters
say: Hi, I'm Arjun.
Chairs read dozens of position papers before every conference, and most of them blur together.
In this lecture, I'll show you a simple structure and a few habits that make yours stand out.

slides.title: The four-part structure
bullets: 1. Background of the topic
2. Past international action
3. Your country's position
4. Proposed solutions
say: A strong paper has four parts.
First, a short background of the topic.
Second, what the international community has already tried.
Third, your country's position, in your country's voice, not yours.
And fourth, the solutions you'll push for in committee.

slides.title: Research that matters
bullets: Your country's voting record and speeches
Relevant treaties and past resolutions
Allies, blocs and red lines
say: Good research starts with your own country.
Look at how it has voted, and what its diplomats have actually said at the UN.
Then find the treaties and resolutions that already exist on the topic.
Finally, map your likely allies and the red lines your country will never cross.

slides.title: Write like a diplomat
bullets: One clear claim per paragraph
Cite facts, with sources
Formal, specific, confident
say: When you write, keep one clear claim in each paragraph.
Back it up with facts, and say where they come from.
Be formal, specific and confident.
Instead of saying your country cares about education, say what it funded, where, and how many students it reached.

slides.title: Solutions chairs notice
bullets: Specific: who does what
Realistic: funded and feasible
Connected to your country's interests
say: Your solutions section is where you win or lose the chair's attention.
Make each proposal specific: who does what, and how it is funded.
Keep it realistic for the UN.
And connect it to your country's interests, because that's what makes it believable in committee.

slides.title: Mistakes to avoid
bullets: Copying Wikipedia or another delegate
Writing your personal opinion
Going over the page limit
say: A few mistakes cost easy marks.
Never copy text, whether from Wikipedia or another delegate.
Don't write your personal opinion; write your country's.
And respect the page limit and the format your conference asks for.

slides.title: Draft it on DelegateDesk
bullets: Background → past action → position → solutions
Use Prep: research briefs with sources
Get chair-style feedback from Coach
say: To recap: background, past action, your position, and your solutions.
On DelegateDesk, the Prep studio builds a research brief with sources, and Coach gives you chair-style feedback on your draft.
Good luck, and happy writing.

lectures.title: Your first opening speech, and points of information
lectures.summary: A sixty-second speech structure, delivery tips, and how to ask and answer points of information.

slides.title: Your first opening speech
bullets: A sixty-second structure
Delivery that sounds confident
Points of information
say: Hello! I'm Sara.
Your opening speech is the first impression you make on the committee and the chairs.
Let's build one together, in sixty seconds or less.

slides.title: The 60-second structure
bullets: Hook: a fact, a story or a question
Position: where your country stands
Proposal: one or two clear ideas
Call to action: invite others to work with you
say: Start with a hook: a striking fact, a short story, or a question.
Then state your country's position in one or two sentences.
Next, give one or two clear proposals.
And finish with a call to action, inviting other delegations to work with you.

slides.title: An example opening
bullets: "Two hundred million children are out of school today."
"Our delegation believes education cannot wait for peace."
"We propose a fund for schools in crisis zones."
say: Here's an example.
Two hundred million children are out of school today.
Our delegation believes education cannot wait for peace.
We propose a dedicated fund for schools in crisis zones, and we invite every delegation in this room to help shape it.

slides.title: Delivery
bullets: Slow down, and pause after key lines
Look up from your notes
End before the gavel
say: How you say it matters as much as what you say.
Slow down, and pause after your most important lines.
Look up from your notes and speak to the room.
And always finish before the chair's gavel, never during it.

slides.title: Points of information
bullets: Ask: short, one question, no speech
Answer: thank them, then answer directly
Don't know? Redirect to your position
say: If a speaker yields to questions, you can ask a point of information.
Keep it short: one clear question, not a speech.
When you answer one, thank the delegate, then answer directly.
If you don't know, calmly bring it back to your country's position.

slides.title: Practise and improve
bullets: Hook → position → proposal → call to action
Time yourself with the speech timer
Rehearse with Practice on DelegateDesk
say: So remember: hook, position, proposal, and a call to action.
Time yourself with the speech timer in DelegateDesk tools, and rehearse with an AI delegation in Practice.
You've got this. See you in committee!
